title: Use of OSI IS-IS for Routing in TCP/IP and Dual Environments
summary: Specifies an integrated routing protocol, based on OSI IS-IS, that can serve as an interior gateway protocol for TCP/IP, OSI, or mixed networks. This lets one routing protocol handle both kinds of traffic. It was developed by the IETF IS-IS working group.

eli5.summary: Delivery drivers need maps. This gives one map style that works for two different kinds of roads at the same time.

questions: what is the difference between level 1 and level 2 is-is
what is ships in the night routing
subtitle: One link-state routing protocol that can carry routes for IP, for OSI, or for both at once.

tldr.problem: Routers that had to forward both TCP/IP and OSI traffic needed routing for each, and the usual approach, called Ships in the Night, runs two completely independent routing protocols side by side.
tldr.mechanism: Integrated IS-IS takes the OSI IS-IS link-state protocol and adds IP-specific fields to its existing packets, so one protocol and one two-level area hierarchy calculate routes for IP-only, OSI-only and dual routers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard, and its metadata lists RFC 1349, RFC 5302 and RFC 5304 as updates. Its only defined authentication is a clear-text password.

today: RFC 1195 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 1349, RFC 5302 and RFC 5304. Its text expects future versions to track the final International Standard version of IS-IS.

sections.title: One Routing Protocol for Two Protocol Suites
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the expectation that TCP/IP and OSI would coexist for an extended period, so there was a critical need for routers to support both kinds of traffic in parallel. There are two main ways to do that. "Ships in the Night" (S.I.N.) runs completely independent routing protocols, for example OSPF for IP and IS-IS for OSI. This RFC specifies the other way: a single integrated protocol for interior routing, meaning route calculation within one routing domain (autonomous system).

It is a companion to the OSI IS-IS specification (ISO DP 10589) and only describes the added features. It was developed by the IETF IS-IS working group. Both kinds of packets are forwarded "as is" over the link layer, with no mutual encapsulation, and the protocol is a dynamic routing protocol based on the SPF (Dijkstra) algorithm.

The RFC defines three router kinds: an IP-only router uses IS-IS for IP and does not otherwise support OSI, an OSI-only router uses IS-IS for OSI as in the base spec, and a dual router uses IS-IS as one protocol for both.
sections.eli5: Instead of hiring two separate mapmakers for two kinds of roads, you hire one who draws both on the same map.

sections.title: The OSI IS-IS Foundation
sections.content:
In IS-IS the network is split into routing domains, and each domain is divided into areas. Level 1 routers know the topology of their own area and send anything for another area to the nearest level 2 router. Level 2 routers know the level 2 topology and which addresses are reachable via each level 2 router, without needing the inside of any area. Only level 2 routers talk to routers outside the domain. The set of level 2 routers must be connected, and there is no provision for repairing a level 2 partition with level 1 links.

OSI addresses explicitly name the area. They split into an Initial Domain Part and a Domain Specific Part, and the combination of the IDP and the high-order part of the DSP is the Area Address.

On a LAN, each router would otherwise report a link to every other router, giving n-squared links. IS-IS instead uses a pseudonode to represent the LAN: each router reports one link to it, and an elected designated router sends the LSP on the pseudonode's behalf. This reduces the potential n-squared links to n links.
sections.eli5: Think of a town with neighborhoods. Local drivers know every street in their neighborhood, and anything going elsewhere goes to the main road driver.

sections.title: How Integrated IS-IS Handles IP
sections.content:
IP uses the same two-level hierarchy as OSI. Each area is IP-only, OSI-only or dual, and there is a single backbone: the RFC does not allow partial overlap of IP and OSI areas, and offers no independent IP and OSI backbones. In a pure IP domain, IP-only and dual routers may be mixed. In a dual domain the mix is per area, a dual area may contain only dual routers, and if both IP and OSI traffic must cross between areas then all level 2 routers must be dual.

Level 1 LSPs list zero or more [IP address, subnet mask, metric] combinations that the router reaches. A destination that matches one is routed by level 1 routing, and otherwise the packet goes to the nearest level 2 router. If a destination matches several entries, the more specific one (more 1 bits in the mask) wins, which the RFC calls "best match" routing. Host routes use a mask of all ones. Default routes use a mask of all zeroes; they are permitted only at level 2 as external routes, and the RFC warns that they can cause black holes.

IP addresses need not be related to the area structure, though the RFC notes that efficiency and scaling are better when there is some correspondence.
sections.eli5: When a driver is not sure where a house is, he picks the street that matches the address best, and sends the rest to the main road driver.

sections.title: Exchanging and Choosing Routes
sections.content:
IS-IS packets carry variable-length fields as code, length and value triplets, each code and length one octet. Unknown codes must be ignored and passed through unchanged, so OSI-only routers ignore IP fields and IP-only routers ignore OSI fields. A "protocols supported" field using one-octet NLPIDs tells neighbors which network protocols a router can relay. IS-IS Hellos list the IP addresses of the sending interface, up to 63 per interface.

To keep level 2 LSPs small, a level 2 router may be manually configured with summary addresses that supersede many level 1 entries. When it instead copies a level 1 entry, the metric is the level 1 metric plus the distance to the level 1 router, and a result above 63 is reported as 63. Packets that match a configured summary but are not reachable by level 1 routing must be discarded.

The RFC fixes an order of preference. Routes inside the area are used before any via level 2. At level 2, routes with internal metrics are always preferred to those with external metrics, then the most specific match, then support for the requested TOS, then the shortest path. Routes learned from OSPF, EGP, RIP or other external protocols are announced as external reachability information.

Optional Type of Service routing uses the IS-IS QOS metrics: delay, expense, error and the default metric. A packet is routed by any one of them, and if no path supports the requested TOS the default metric is used.
sections.eli5: Drivers write down the streets they can reach and how far each is. When two roads fit, they choose the closer match first, and the shorter trip second.

sections.title: NSAP Addresses for IP-Only Routers
sections.content:
IS-IS packet formats require OSI-style addresses for routers, even IP-only ones, where they are used only inside IS-IS. The RFC recommends getting normal NSAP assignments even in pure IP domains, because this eases a later move to dual operation.

Where that is not wanted, an address compatible with the GOSIP version 2.0 format can be built: AFI 47, ICD 00 05, a DFI and 3-octet AA for this special IP-only use, 2 reserved octets of 00 00, a 2-octet routing domain field holding the autonomous system number, a 2-octet Area, a 6-octet ID and a 1-octet SEL. The ID should be a unique IEEE 802 48-bit station ID, or the hex value 02 00 placed before the router's IP address. All routers in an area must share the same high-order part of the address.
sections.eli5: The map system wants every driver to have a special badge number, so drivers who only know street addresses get a badge made from their street address.

sections.title: The Six New Fields
sections.content:
The packet types are the same as in IS-IS and all fixed fields stay the same. IS-IS has Hello packets, Link State Packets and Sequence Number Packets (complete and partial, as a kind of acknowledgement and request). The integrated protocol adds six variable-length fields.

  • Protocols Supported (code 129) must be in all Hellos and in LSP number 0 from IP-capable routers. If it is missing, the sender is assumed to be OSI-only.
  • IP Interface Address (code 132) holds 4-octet addresses.
  • Authentication Information (code 133) is optional.
  • IP Internal Reachability Information (code 128) and IP External Reachability Information (code 130) hold entries with a default metric, optional delay, expense and error metrics, an IP address and a subnet mask, so the length is a multiple of 12. Neither may appear in pseudonode LSPs.
  • Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information (code 131) is carried in level 2 LSPs for the convenience of an external routing protocol, for example so border routers can find each other.

The ISO draft did not allow variable-length fields in sequence number packets, so the RFC uses a corrected encoding, given in an annex.
sections.eli5: Each Hello or update gets a few new labeled boxes: what languages I speak, my address, my password, and the streets I can reach.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Any IS-IS packet may carry authentication information, and the mechanism is extensible. The only mechanism defined is a simple password sent in the clear without encryption. The RFC says plainly that it gives no useful protection against intentional misbehavior and should be seen as weak protection against accidental errors such as misconfiguration. The password is set per link for Hellos, per area for level 1 packets and per domain for level 2 packets, with a transmit password and a set of receive passwords so it can be changed gracefully. Other security aspects are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The only lock is a password written on the outside of the envelope, so it only stops honest mistakes, not sneaky people.

viz.caption: THE THREE ROUTER KINDS IN RFC 1195
CODES OF THE NEW IS-IS FIELDS

items.label: IP Internal Reachability
items.desc: Addresses inside the domain reached directly; length a multiple of 12.

items.label: Protocols Supported
items.desc: One NLPID octet per protocol the router can relay.

items.label: IP External Reachability
items.desc: Addresses outside the domain; level 2 only; length a multiple of 12.

items.label: Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information
items.desc: Carried transparently through level 2 for border routers.

items.label: Authentication Information
items.desc: Optional; used to authenticate the packet.
